hero.name: Varun
hero.who: a young sales executive in Gurugram who snoozes daily and starts every morning rushed

story.b: Varun's alarm rings at 7:00. He hits snooze. Then 7:10, 7:20, 7:30, 7:40. At 7:45 he jumps up in panic, skips his bath, pulls on yesterday's shirt and runs to the metro station with toothpaste still on his lip. Breakfast is a bread pakora eaten standing at a stall near his office. At the 9:30 sales meeting he is already irritated, and he snaps at a junior who asks a simple question. At night he scrolls on his phone till 1 a.m., just to feel some time is his. The next morning the snoozing starts again. His flatmate Gaurav jokes that Varun's mornings look like a chase scene. Varun does not find it funny anymore.

ask.q: Varun's rushed mornings leave him irritable all day. What is the most useful change to try first?
o: Drink extra coffee at office to push through the bad mood
Start the day with a short, calm slice of time for himself
Set the alarm for 4:30 and begin a two-hour routine from tomorrow
ask.why: Coffee hides the grumpiness but leaves the rushed start untouched. A sudden two-hour routine at 4:30 would cut into his sleep and would likely collapse within days. A short, calm start sets a steadier tone for the whole day, and he can build from there.

chapters.take: How you start your morning quietly shapes how the rest of the day goes.

story.b: Varun makes one small change. He sets his alarm for 6:45 instead of 7:00, and to protect his sleep he leaves his phone charging in the hall from 11:30 at night. The extra fifteen minutes are only for him. He makes chai, sits on the small balcony and watches the auto drivers gather at the corner. No phone, no emails. That is all. On the first day it feels pointless. By the fourth day he notices he reaches the metro walking, not running. In the sales meeting he listens properly and answers his junior with patience. Nothing big has changed at work, but the day no longer starts by chasing Varun, and the rest of it follows that calmer tone.

ask.q: Varun wants to wake fifteen minutes earlier, but he often sleeps late. What should he do?
o: Move his bedtime earlier too, so the new wake-up does not cost him sleep
Wake earlier anyway and catch up on sleep during the weekends
Keep his late nights, since fifteen minutes less sleep will hardly matter
ask.why: An earlier start only helps if he is rested. Cutting sleep, even a little each night, can leave him more tired and grumpy, and weekend catch-up may not make up for it. Shifting bedtime keeps his rest intact. If sleep stays hard, a doctor is worth seeing.

chapters.take: A calm start, even a short one, can change the tone of your whole day.

story.b: Some mornings the snooze button still wins. Varun notices the problem starts the second his hand finds the phone beside his pillow. So he tries something new. Before sleeping, he tells himself tomorrow will be a good morning, and he gives himself one reason: a calm chai before work. He places the phone on top of the steel cupboard across the room, next to a full bottle of water. When the alarm rings, he has to stand up and walk. He drinks half the bottle right there, then goes straight to brush his teeth. By the time he is done, the urge to crawl back into bed has mostly gone. Excuses, Varun notices, work best on a body lying down.

ask.q: Gaurav says he will stop snoozing by simply being more disciplined. What would help him more?
o: Set five alarms a few minutes apart so one of them finally works
Rely on willpower and promise himself never to press snooze again
Keep the alarm across the room and plan a few simple steps after standing up
ask.why: Half-asleep willpower is very weak, so promises usually lose to a warm bed. Many alarms just train him to snooze more. Placing the alarm out of reach and following quick physical steps, like water and brushing, pulls him out of autopilot before his excuses start.

chapters.take: Make the first moves physical and planned, before your excuses wake up.

story.b: Varun's team has a big pitch to a hospital chain on Thursday, and he is presenting. On Wednesday morning his mind is already racing. He uses his fifteen minutes differently. First, two minutes sitting still on the balcony, just breathing and listening to pressure cookers whistle in other flats. Then he says a few plain lines to himself about the salesperson he is becoming: prepared, honest, calm with tough questions. Finally he closes his eyes and runs through the pitch in his mind, walking in, opening the laptop, answering the price question without rushing. It feels a little silly. But on Thursday, when the client's finance head interrupts, Varun realises he has already rehearsed this moment, and his voice stays steady.

ask.q: Before a tough client call, Varun's junior Priya feels panicky. What should Varun suggest?
o: A few quiet minutes, then picturing the call going well step by step
Scrolling the client's social media till the last minute to feel ready
Not thinking about the call at all so she does not get nervous
ask.why: Last-minute scrolling feeds the panic with more noise, and avoiding the call leaves her unprepared. A short pause calms her mind, and walking through the call in her imagination, including the tough moments, helps her arrive steady and intentional instead of reactive.

chapters.take: A few quiet minutes and a clear picture of the day make you steady, not reactive.

story.b: After a month, Varun adds three more small pieces. He climbs to the terrace for three minutes of skipping, which wakes him faster than any coffee. He reads five pages of a book on listening skills while his chai cools. And he writes three lines in a cheap diary: one thing he is grateful for, one lesson from yesterday, one aim for today. To make room, he moves his bedtime to 11:00 and his alarm to 6:30, so his sleep stays the same. The diary surprises him most. Flipping back after two weeks, Varun sees lessons he had already forgotten, like letting clients finish their sentences. The five pages add up too. By month's end he finishes the book, a first since college.

ask.q: Varun has only ten minutes for moving, reading and writing each morning. Which plan makes most sense?
o: Skip them all until he can find a full free hour
Do a few minutes of each every day and let them add up
Pick only reading and do one long session on Sundays
ask.why: Waiting for a free hour usually means waiting forever. A long Sunday session misses the daily rhythm that makes these habits work. A few minutes each of moving, reading and writing are small enough to keep, and small daily doses add up faster than expected.

chapters.take: A few minutes of moving, reading and writing each day add up quickly.

story.b: In his second month, Varun is sent on a four-day sales trip to Lucknow. Early trains and late client dinners break his routine on the first day. Instead of dropping it, he shrinks it. Ten minutes in the hotel room: one minute of silence, two minutes of stretching, two pages, and a single line in the diary. Back home, his cousin Tanya, who works night shifts at a customer support centre, asks how she could ever have a morning routine. Varun suggests she does her own version after she wakes in the afternoon. The time of day matters less than doing it regularly. Tanya tries it the next day with her three o'clock chai, and sends him a photo of her diary.

ask.q: Tanya works night shifts and sleeps till 2 p.m. How can she best use the morning routine idea?
o: Force herself awake at 6 a.m. on days off to do it properly
Give up, since the routine only works for people with day jobs
Do a short version after she wakes, keeping both her sleep and the habit
ask.why: Forcing a 6 a.m. start would cut into her sleep, which matters more than any routine. Giving up misses the point, since the idea is to start her own day well, whenever that is. A short version after waking fits her life, and consistency is what makes it stick.

chapters.take: A routine that fits your real life, even ten minutes long, beats a perfect one you cannot keep.

story.b: Ten weeks later, Varun still does not love alarms, but he no longer fights them. The phone sits on the cupboard with the water bottle beside it, and most mornings he is on the balcony by 6:40 with chai, a few quiet minutes, five pages and three lines in his diary. Some days it is the ten-minute version. He sleeps by eleven, and the 1 a.m. scrolling has faded. At work, his team lead mentions that Varun seems steadier in client meetings. Gaurav has noticed the change too, mostly because Varun now has time to make two cups of chai. The metro is still crowded, but Varun walks to the station instead of running.

chapters.take: Calm mornings come from small steady habits and enough sleep, not heroic alarms.
